The mass of an upper half-disk $D$ of radius $3$ centered at the origin with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }\lambda (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/d8e2f73ce8840471143689748e188debaf5fde8f3aaf5021fd8d99c4f86a72d6.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Finally, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\frac{81}{4}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{4}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{4}(-(-1)+1) \\  & =\frac{81}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the upper half-disk is $M=\frac{81}{2}.$
